docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the hub subsystem of RadioLink, Team 105's embedded project. It is written so the design can be reviewed on its own, without the team report open beside it.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: RadioLink is a hub-and-spoke system, and this board is the hub. It has an on-board OLED for graphics, a debug LED, and three UART ports. Board 1 carries the microphone, board 2 carries the pushbuttons and a temperature sensor, and board 3 carries the speaker. The microphone and button boards send their data to the hub. The hub shows a custom interface on the OLED, which is navigated with board 2's buttons, and it plays the microphone signal through the speaker.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My work on RadioLink has centered on concept ideation, user-needs benchmarking, and the hub itself. The hub receives the microphone and temperature data, presents it on a custom OLED interface that is navigated with the pushbuttons, and sends the microphone signal to the speaker.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram is the hub subsystem of RadioLink, Team 105's hub-and-spoke design. A Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano sits at the center. A computer supplies 5 V over USB. An LM7805 provides a regulated 5 V rail rated for 1 A, and a separate 3.3 V regulator rated for 500 mA powers the display.

The microcontroller drives a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED (ER-OLED0.96-1.3W) over I2C. SDA is RB2 and SCL is RB1. The OLED side of that bus is 3.3 V, and the microcontroller side is 5 V. A red LED is driven from RA2 using PWM.

Three UART ports connect this hub to the other boards. Each link is 5 V and uses an RX/TX pair:

  • Connector 1: RX on RC3, TX on RC2
  • Connector 2: RX on RF1, TX on RF0
  • Connector 3: RX on RA4, TX on RA3

These ports connect to the microphone board, the button and temperature board, and the speaker board. The microphone and button boards send data in. The hub shows temperature readings and the audio path on the OLED, and it sends the microphone signal out to the speaker.

docs.text:
• $2.49 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Common SSD1306 controller Small 0.96-inch display Many libraries and examples available Requires 1 KB framebuffer Low cost Easy to implement Fast shipping

Choice: Option 3: ER-OLED0.96-1.3W

Rationale: Option 3 is inexpensive, easy to implement, and available quickly. The SSD1306 is well documented and has many open-source libraries, making PIC integration easier. The 0.96-inch display is small, but it should be readable for a handheld device. Options 1 and 2 have lead times of 16 and 12 weeks.

docs.title: Voltage Regulator
docs.text: Requirements: Convert a 9 V supply to 5 V for the hub and its UART links to the microphone, button, and speaker boards.

docs.text:

Pros Cons Widely used 7805 regulator Wastes power as heat Extensive documentation Large TO-220 package High DigiKey stock 5 V output from 9 V input Up to 1.5 A output Easy to prototype

docs.text:
• ~$0.65 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Very low quiescent current 250 mA maximum output Good for battery operation Harder to breadboard or hand solder Accepts up to 13.2 V input Less common than the 7805 family High DigiKey stock Small SOT-23 package

docs.title: Option 3: MC7805CDTRKG (onsemi)
docs.text:
• ~$0.49 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Widely used 7805 family Wastes power as heat Low cost Harder to breadboard Good DigiKey availability Higher quiescent current than MCP1702 Up to 1 A output Compact DPAK package

Choice: Option 1: L7805CV

Rationale: Option 1 is widely used, well documented, and readily available. Its 1.5 A output also provides plenty of current for the circuit. The through-hole package makes it easy to prototype.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is the hub subsystem of RadioLink for Team 105. It is centered on a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The hub reads the microphone board and the button and temperature board over UART, shows that information on a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED, sends the microphone signal to the speaker board, and drives a local debug LED.

Power comes from a 9 V barrel jack. A 1 A fuse feeds an LM7805, which regulates that input to 5 V for the microcontroller and the UART connectors. A separate 3.3 V supply powers the OLED. BSS138 level shifters translate the I2C signals between the 5 V microcontroller and the 3.3 V display. Test points, a pushbutton, and the red LED provide debugging access on the microcontroller side. Three 8-pin connectors carry the UART links to the other subsystems.

Figure 1: Hub subsystem schematic for RadioLink, showing the microcontroller and debug circuitry, the OLED and I2C interface, 9 V input and 5 V regulation, and the three UART connectors.
